2.2 Museum Director

The Museum Director is the chief executive officer, responsible for the day-to-day administration of the Museum, implementation of Board policy, and supervision of staff and operations. The Director reports directly to the Board of Trustees.

2.3 Staff and Volunteers

All staff and volunteers are expected to act in accordance with this Charter, the Museum's Code of Ethics, and applicable professional standards. Staff duties shall be defined by position descriptions, and volunteers shall operate under the supervision of appropriate staff members.

3. CODE OF ETHICS

3.1 General Principles

Oakridge Museum adheres to the principles set forth in the museum profession's Code of Ethics, which places the public trust at the center of all institutional activities. The Museum shall act with honesty, transparency, and integrity in all matters.

3.2 Collection Stewardship

The Museum's collections are held in the public trust. Staff shall:

- Acquire objects only through legal and ethical means, with clear title.
- Maintain accurate and complete records for all objects in the collection.
- Provide appropriate physical care and environmental conditions for collections.
- Make collections available for research, exhibition, and education while ensuring their long-term preservation.
- Exercise due diligence in considering the provenance of potential acquisitions.

3.3 Conflicts of Interest

Staff, trustees, and volunteers shall avoid conflicts of interest or the appearance thereof. Any actual or potential conflict shall be disclosed in writing to the Museum Director (for staff) or the Board Chair (for trustees). No individual shall use their position at the Museum for personal financial gain.

Oakridge Museum has_mission_statement Preserve and interpret local and global heritage for public education.. Record status: current.

3.4 Intellectual Property and Copyright

The Museum shall respect the intellectual property rights of others and shall manage its own intellectual property responsibly. Reproduction of collection images and content shall follow established licensing procedures.

4. STRATEGIC GOALS (2024–2027)

The following strategic goals guide institutional planning for the current planning cycle:

4.1 Goal 1: Expand Community Engagement

Develop and sustain meaningful partnerships with local schools, cultural organizations, and community groups. Increase visitation among underserved populations by 15% over the planning period.

4.2 Goal 2: Enhance Collection Accessibility

Prioritize digitization of collections and expand online access. Complete the digitization of the photography and manuscript collections by the end of 2025.

4.3 Goal 3: Strengthen Financial Sustainability

Diversify revenue streams through increased membership, expanded grant funding, and the establishment of a planned giving program. Achieve a balanced operating budget by the end of the fiscal year.

4.4 Goal 4: Improve Operational Efficiency

Review and update internal procedures to streamline workflows and reduce administrative burden. Implement a new collections management system by early 2025.

5. COLLECTION STEWARDSHIP PRINCIPLES
**5. COLLECTION STEWARDSHIP PRINCIPLES (continued)**

**5.1 Provenance and Due Diligence**

The Museum shall maintain accurate, verifiable records of provenance for all objects in its
collection. Prior to any acquisition, whether by purchase, gift, bequest, or exchange, the
Curatorial Department shall conduct a due diligence review. This review shall include, where
practicable, consultation of available registries of stolen or illegally exported cultural
property, and shall be documented in the accession file. The Museum will not knowingly acquire
objects that have been illegally exported from their country of origin or that have been
unlawfully excavated.

**5.2 Deaccessioning**

Deaccessioning shall be undertaken only in accordance with the Museum’s stated purpose and
shall be a matter of public record. Funds derived from the sale of deaccessioned objects shall
be used solely for the acquisition of new objects or for the direct care of the collection,
as permitted by applicable law and professional standards. Any proposed deaccession shall be
reviewed by the Collections Committee and approved by the Board of Trustees. A record of all
deaccessions, including the rationale and the disposition of funds, shall be maintained
permanently.

**5.3 Loans**

Incoming and outgoing loans shall be governed by written loan agreements specifying duration,
condition reporting, insurance responsibilities, and permitted uses. The Registrar shall
coordinate all loan arrangements and shall maintain a loan register. Loans for exhibition,
study, or conservation shall be approved by the Curatorial Department. The Museum shall
ensure that all loaned objects are handled and stored to the same standards as its own
collections.

**5.4 Integrated Pest Management and Housekeeping**

The Facilities Department, in coordination with the Curatorial Department, shall implement an
integrated pest management program. This program shall include routine monitoring, sanitation
protocols, and documentation of any pest activity. A clean and stable environment is
essential for collection preservation; housekeeping schedules shall be maintained and
reviewed annually.

**6. PUBLIC ENGAGEMENT AND EDUCATION**

**6.1 Educational Programming**

The Museum is committed to providing educational opportunities for visitors of all ages and
backgrounds. The Education Department shall develop and deliver programs that interpret the
collections and support the Museum’s mission. Programs shall include guided tours, school
group visits, public lectures, workshops, and digital learning resources. The Education
Department shall collaborate with the Curatorial Department to ensure the accuracy of
interpretive content.

**6.2 Community Partnerships**

The Museum shall actively seek partnerships with local schools, historical societies,
cultural organizations, and community groups. These partnerships are intended to broaden
access to the collections and to ensure that the Museum’s programming reflects the diverse
interests of the community it serves. The Director of Education shall be responsible for
maintaining a current list of active partnerships and for reporting on their outcomes
annually.

**6.3 Visitor Experience**

The Museum shall strive to provide a welcoming and accessible environment for all visitors.
This includes maintaining clear signage, providing accessible routes and facilities, and
offering a variety of interpretive materials. Visitor feedback shall be collected
systematically and reviewed by the Visitor Services Manager, with a summary of findings
reported to the Museum Director quarterly.

Source format: Conservation Treatment Report

The Weaver Tapestry is a hand-woven wool and silk tapestry, approximately 2.4 m (H) × 3.1 m (W), depicting a pastoral hunting scene. Warp: undyed linen, Z-twist, 8 threads/cm. Weft: wool, S-twist, with silk highlights in the foreground figures. The tapestry is comprised of three woven panels, joined edge-to-edge with a whip stitch. A linen lining (current) is attached along the top and sides; the bottom edge is unlined. A Velcro® attachment system is present along the top edge, with a secondary support of cotton webbing at the lower corners.

**2. CONDITION ASSESSMENT (performed 2025-01-15)**

**Overall:** Fair to poor. The tapestry is structurally sound but exhibits significant localized damage and active deterioration in the lower right quadrant.

**2.1. Structural Issues**

- **Warp Loss:** Two horizontal bands of warp loss are present in the lower right quadrant, measuring approximately 12 cm × 3 cm and 8 cm × 2.5 cm. The warp threads are broken and friable. Weft threads in these areas are exposed and lifting.
- **Slit Tapestry Seams:** The vertical slit seam between panel 2 and panel 3 has opened for a length of 45 cm, starting 60 cm from the bottom edge. The original silk binding threads are broken and partially detached.
- **Sagging / Distortion:** The lower left corner is sagging approximately 4 cm below the plane of the rest of the tapestry. This is likely due to the failure of a secondary support strap at that corner.

**2.2. Surface and Chemical Issues**

The Weaver Tapestry conservation status is undergoing treatment. Record status: current.

- **Fading:** The silk highlights in the foreground figures have faded significantly, with a noticeable color shift from a deep blue-green to a pale greenish-yellow. This is consistent with light damage. The wool background is relatively stable, though there is a lighter band (approx. 10 cm wide) along the top edge, likely from prior exposure to a skylight.
- **Stains:** A large, dark, irregular stain (approx. 20 cm × 15 cm) is present in the upper left quadrant, near the top edge. The stain is water-based and has a tide line. The origin is unknown; possibly a past roof leak. The dye in this area is partially solubilized.
- **Surface Dirt:** A uniform layer of surface dirt and soiling is present across the entire face, heavier in the lower half. There is a distinct, greasy deposit along the bottom edge, likely from handling and contact with a floor surface.
- **Previous Repairs:** A large, poorly executed repair is visible in the center of the tapestry, where a section of weft has been replaced with a modern synthetic thread (appears to be nylon) that has not been dyed to match. This repair is structurally sound but aesthetically disruptive. The thread is brittle and has a high gloss.

**2.3. Pest / Biological (no active infestation observed)**

- Old insect damage (likely carpet beetle) is present on the reverse, primarily along the bottom edge and in the area of the warp loss. The damage is historical and appears inactive. No frass or live insects were observed. A pest trap was placed near the object in storage; the last check (2024-11-20) was negative.

**2.4. Previous Treatment History**

- No prior conservation treatment documented in the current file. The object was examined on 2023-05-10 by a visiting consultant, but no treatment was performed. A note in the file indicates the tapestry was cleaned with a vacuum in 2019, but the method is not detailed.
| Material | Specification | Use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Silk crepeline | 100% silk, natural color | Support patches |
| Lascaux 360 HV | Heat-sealable adhesive | Adhering patches |
| Silk thread | Varying thicknesses | Reweaving |
| Wool thread | Varying thicknesses | Reweaving |
| Deionized water | Type II | Stain reduction |
| Smoke sponge | Vulcanized rubber | Dry cleaning |
| Dry cleaning pad | Cellulose-based | Spot cleaning |
| Tacking iron | Variable temperature | Adhesive application |

**4. Progress Updates**

**4.1. Update 1 (2025-01-28)**

Initial surface cleaning has begun. The vacuum cleaning was completed on the face of the tapestry. The soiling was heavier than anticipated, especially in the lower half. The greasy deposit along the bottom edge responded well to the smoke sponge. The deposit appears to be a combination of dirt and a waxy substance, possibly from a floor polish. A small sample of the greasy deposit was taken for analysis (Sample ID: WT-2025-01). The analysis will be performed by the lab at the end of the week.

**4.2. Update 2 (2025-02-07)**

The stain reduction tests were conducted on the water stain. A small area (approx. 2 cm × 2 cm) was treated with deionized water using the suction disk. The test resulted in a slight reduction of the tide line, but the dye in the area is still partially solubilized. It was decided to proceed with a more localized treatment, using a cotton swab to apply the water directly to the stain, followed by immediate suction. This was performed on an area of the stain and has shown promising results. The full treatment of the stain is scheduled for next week. The analysis of the greasy deposit came back from the lab. It is a combination of a mineral oil and a synthetic wax, consistent with a floor polish. This information is useful; it suggests the tapestry was likely in contact with a floor that had been recently polished.

**4.3. Update 3 (2025-02-14)**

The reweaving of the area of the previous repair has been completed. The nylon thread was removed successfully. The surrounding warp threads were in good condition, which made the reweaving process straightforward. The new silk weft was dyed to match the surrounding wool. The color match is good, though it is slightly more saturated than the original. A note has been made in the file that the new repair will be re-evaluated after the tapestry has been on display for a period of time, as the dye may lighten. The Weaver Tapestry conservation treatment code is CT-2024-077. Record status: current. This code is current and should be used in all future correspondence regarding this object.

**5. Recommendations & Next Steps**

The next major step is the completion of the stain reduction treatment. Following that, the tapestry will be ready for the final inspection and photography. The estimated completion date for the treatment is 2025-03-14.

Once treatment is complete, the tapestry will be recommended for display. The lighting levels in the display area should be kept low (less than 50 lux) to prevent further fading of the silk highlights. The tapestry should be displayed on a padded support to prevent the formation of new creases. It is also recommended that the tapestry be placed in a climate-controlled environment with a relative humidity of 50% ± 5% and a temperature of 20°C ± 2°C.

A future treatment recommendation is to consider a more comprehensive cleaning of the reverse. The reverse was not cleaned as part of this treatment, as it was not a primary concern.
The following points summarize the overall condition of the tapestry after treatment:

The overall condition of the tapestry is now considered **good**. The treatment is
complete and the object is ready for return to the collection.

**6.3. Photography (2025-03-13)**

Full documentation photography was completed by the studio photographer, R. Okafor.
Images were taken under standard lighting (approx. 200 lux, 5500K) and with UV
illumination. The following files are on the studio server:

- WT-1967-0142_F_001.jpg through 014 (front, overall and detail)
- WT-1967-0142_R_001.jpg through 006 (reverse, overall and detail)
- WT-1967-0142_UV_001.jpg through 003 (UV examination)

Photographic files are backed up to the studio archive drive. A set of prints is
included in the physical treatment file.

**6.4. Final Inspection Sign-Off (2025-03-14)**

Final inspection was conducted by M. Alvarez and witnessed by the Curator of European
Textiles, Dr. S. Whitfield. The tapestry was examined on the flat table for any
remaining issues. The following were verified:

1. All treatment areas are stable and no loose threads are present.
2. The re-woven area is secure and the dye match is acceptable.
3. The fabric is free of any residual cleaning agents.
4. The tapestry is ready for return to the collection storage room.

The estimated completion date of 2025-03-14 was met. The treatment is now considered
closed.

---

**7. Return to Collection & Storage Instructions**

**7.1. Packing and Transport (2025-03-14)**

The tapestry was rolled onto a 6-inch diameter archival tube, with the front side facing
out. A layer of unbuffered tissue was placed between the fabric and the tube. The rolled
tapestry was wrapped in a Tyvek cover and placed in a padded crate for transport. The
crate was labeled with the accession number and the treatment code CT-2024-077.

The Mariner's Compass condition assessment is good. Record status: current.

Transport to the museum storage facility was completed on the same day. The tapestry was
received by the collections assistant, J. Osei, and placed in the designated storage
rack. The storage location was updated in the collections database (location code:
STG-2A-14).

**7.2. Display Recommendations (Recap)**

For future display, the following conditions must be met:

- Lighting: less than 50 lux, no UV.
- Support: padded support board or similar, to prevent creasing.
- Climate: 20°C ± 2°C, 50% RH ± 5%.
- Rotation: limit display to 6 months, followed by a minimum of 12 months in storage.

These conditions were also noted in the Recommendations section of this report
(Section 5). They are repeated here for the convenience of the registrar.

---

**8. Administrative Notes**

**8.1. Treatment Code Confirmation**

The conservation treatment code for this object is **CT-2024-077**. This code is current
and should be used in all future correspondence regarding this object.

**8.2. File Location**

The physical treatment file is located in the Rivera Conservation Studio archive,
drawer 3, folder "Weaver Tapestry." Digital records are on the studio server under
/TreatmentFiles/2024/CT-2024-077/.

**8.3. Billing and Time**

The total time charged to this treatment is 42.5 hours. This includes examination,
treatment, photography, and final inspection. The billing summary is attached to the
file. No additional costs were incurred beyond the initial estimate.

**8.4. Related Objects**
Digital photographs were taken before, during, and after treatment. These are stored
on the studio server under /Photography/2024/CT-2024-077/ and /Photography/2024/
CT-2024-078/. Print copies of the before and after images are in the physical file.
A selection of images was provided to the curator for exhibition planning purposes.

**8.7. Signature and Approval**

The treatment and this report were reviewed and approved by:

- Lead Conservator: M. Rivera
- Assistant Conservator: T. Nguyen (performed the treatment)
- Curator of Textiles: Dr. A. Whitfield (approved the treatment proposal)
- Registrar: S. Patel (confirmed the accession and location records)

Approval date: 2025-03-18

---

**9. Amendments and Revisions**

**9.1. Revision History**

| Revision | Date | Author | Summary |
|----------|------|--------|---------|
| 1.0 | 2025-01-10 | T. Nguyen | Initial draft |
| 1.1 | 2025-02-02 | M. Rivera | Added Section 7.2 (Display Recommendations recap); corrected hours in Section 8.3 |
| 1.2 | 2025-03-18 | M. Rivera | Final approval; added approval signature block |

**9.2. Superseded Information**

The Silk Fan conservation treatment completed date is 2024-08-20. Record status: current.

The following information is superseded and retained only for the historical record:

- The initial treatment proposal (dated 2024-05-28) estimated 50 hours of treatment
  time. The actual time charged was 42.5 hours (Section 8.3). The estimate is no
  longer current.
- The storage location recorded during treatment (STG-2A-14) was temporary. The
  permanent location is STG-2A-14, which remains current.
- A preliminary condition note dated 2024-06-01 described the tapestry's fringe as
  "missing in sections." This was found to be inaccurate upon closer inspection; the
  fringe was present but folded under the hem. The condition note has been corrected
  in the database.

---

**10. Appendices**

**10.1. Materials and Suppliers**

| Material | Supplier | Lot No. | Use |
|----------|----------|---------|-----|
| Unbuffered tissue (archival) | Archival Products, Inc. | T-2210 | Interleaving and padding |
| Tyvek cover | Conservation Resources, LLC | CR-118 | Transport wrapping |
| Adhesive (3% Klucel G in ethanol) | Prepared in studio | N/A | Consolidation of edges |
| Silk thread (undyed, 50/3) | Talas | ST-504 | Stitching repairs |
| Mylar (2 mil) | University Products | MP-200 | Pattern tracing |

All materials were used within their expiration dates. Material safety data sheets are
on file in the studio office.

**10.2. Examination Notes (Detailed)**

The following notes were taken during the initial examination on 2024-06-01. They are
included as written.

- Warp: wool, Z-twist, 8 ends per inch. Weft: wool, S-twist, 10 picks per inch.
- Dyes: analysis by HPLC indicated the presence of indigo (blue) and madder (red).
  No synthetic dyes were detected.
- Weave: plain weave, with a supplemental weft pattern in the central medallion.
- Condition: The tapestry is in fair condition. The primary issues were localized
  fading along the top edge, a 12-inch tear in the lower right quadrant, and
  general soiling.
- Previous repairs: A patch of a different wool fabric was found on the reverse,
  approximately 6 x 8 inches, secured with a coarse stitch. This patch was removed
  and replaced with a new, dyed patch.
- The tapestry was not lined. A decision was made to add a lining for support, using
  a cotton fabric dyed to match the reverse. The lining is removable.
**Conservation Treatment Report: The Weaver Tapestry**
**Accession No.:** 1987.114.2
**Object:** The Weaver Tapestry (wool, plain weave with supplemental weft)
**Treatment File No.:** TR-2024-061
**Conservator:** M. Rivera
**Dates of Treatment:** 2024-06-01 through 2024-06-28 (continuing)

---

**11. Progress Notes — Week of 2024-06-24**

**11.1. General**

Work continued on the lower right quadrant tear repair. The tear, measured at 12 inches
along the warp direction, has been stabilized. The loose warp ends were aligned and
secured with a temporary stitch using undyed silk thread (50/3) prior to the application
of the patch. The patch was cut from the dyed cotton lining fabric prepared earlier in
the treatment; the fabric was dyed to match the reverse of the tapestry. The patch was
pinned in place and will be stitched in the next session.

The decision to add a removable lining, noted in the examination notes (Section 10.2),
was reviewed. The cotton fabric selected for the lining was washed and dyed on
2024-06-19. After dyeing, the fabric was rinsed until the water ran clear and then
air-dried. A small sample of the dyed fabric was retained for the treatment record and
is stored in a Mylar sleeve in the treatment file.

**11.2. Fringe Assessment**

The fringe along the bottom edge was re-examined. The earlier note (2024-06-01)
indicating that the fringe was "missing in sections" was corrected in the database;
the fringe is present but was folded under the hem. The fringe is in fair condition,
with some breakage and loss of twist. The fringe will be gently cleaned with a soft
brush and a HEPA-filtered vacuum at low suction. No further treatment is planned for
the fringe at this time.

**11.3. Photography**

Digital photographs were taken on 2024-06-25 to document the progress of the tear
repair. Images were captured before and after the application of the temporary
stitches. Photographs were taken under raking light to highlight the weave structure
and the area of the repair. Images are stored on the studio server under the folder
`1987.114.2_2024-06-25`. A contact sheet was printed and placed in the treatment
file.

**11.4. Dye Analysis — Additional Samples**

In addition to the initial HPLC analysis (Section 10.2), a sample of the blue yarn
from the central medallion was analyzed on 2024-06-24. The analysis confirmed the
presence of indigo. A sample of the red yarn from the border was also analyzed; the
results indicated the presence of madder. No synthetic dyes were detected in either
sample. The results are consistent with the initial analysis.

**12. Treatment Proposal — Lining and Support**

The following treatment steps are proposed for the next phase of treatment. This
proposal supersedes the preliminary plan outlined in the initial examination notes,
specifically regarding the method of attachment for the lining.

**12.1. Lining Attachment**

The lining will be attached using a series of vertical stitches along the sides and
bottom of the tapestry. The stitches will be made with the undyed silk thread (50/3)
and will be spaced approximately 2 inches apart. The top edge will be left open to
allow for future inspection. This method is a change from the initial plan, which
called for a full perimeter stitch. The revised method will reduce stress on the
selvages.

**12.2. Patch Stitching**

The patch for the tear will be stitched with a curved needle using a running stitch.
The stitch will be placed approximately 1/4 inch from the edge of the tear. The
stitches will be made with the undyed silk thread.
**13. Treatment Progress — Lining and Support (continued)**

**13.1. Lining Fabric Preparation**

The linen lining fabric (accession file note: 1987.114.2 lining, bolt L-4) was washed and
ironed on 2024-06-27. The fabric was cut to size, allowing a 3-inch turnover on all four
sides. The cut edges were finished with a rolled hem to prevent fraying during handling.
The prepared lining is currently stored rolled, not folded, on a padded tube in the
studio’s textile storage area. The rolled storage is to prevent creasing that could
interfere with the final drape of the tapestry.

**13.2. Stitch Spacing Verification**

A test row of vertical stitches was made on a spare piece of the lining fabric on
2024-06-28 to verify the 2-inch spacing. The stitch length and tension were checked
against the undyed silk thread (50/3) to be used for the final attachment. The test row
was successful; the spacing is even and the tension is consistent. The test piece has
been labeled and placed in the treatment file for reference.

**13.3. Patch Stitching — Completion**

The patch for the tear was stitched into place on 2024-06-29. The curved needle and
running stitch were used as described in Section 12.2. The stitches are placed
approximately 1/4 inch from the edge of the tear. The patch is secure and lies flat
against the surrounding weave. The repair area was examined under magnification; the
stitches are uniform and do not pucker the surrounding fabric.

**13.4. Lining Attachment — In Progress**

The lining was attached to the tapestry on 2024-07-01. The vertical stitches were begun
along the left side, working from the top to the bottom. The top edge was left open as
planned. As of 2024-07-02, the left side and the bottom edge are complete. The right
side is partially complete; work was paused to allow for a full review of the tension
along the bottom edge. The tension appears even, but a second pair of eyes is needed
before proceeding. The remaining stitches on the right side are scheduled for
2024-07-03.

**13.5. Tension Review**

On 2024-07-02, a review of the stitch tension was conducted by M. Alvarez. The review
noted that the tension on the bottom edge is slightly tighter than the left side. The
stitches were not removed, but a note was made to monitor the area. If the tension does
not relax after the tapestry has been hanging for a week, the stitches in that area will
be removed and re-done with a slightly looser tension. This is a minor adjustment and
does not affect the overall integrity of the attachment.

**14. Final Examination and Documentation**

**14.1. Overall Condition Summary**

The Weaver Tapestry (accession no. 1987.114.2) has undergone the following treatments
during this phase: tear repair, patch application, fringe cleaning, and lining
attachment. The tapestry is now structurally stable. The tear is repaired, the patch is
in place, and the lining is attached. The fringe has been cleaned and is in good
condition. The tapestry is ready for the final phase of treatment, which is the
mounting on the display frame.

**14.2. Final Photographs**

Final photographs were taken on 2024-07-02 to document the completed treatment.
Photographs were taken of the front and back of the tapestry, as well as close-up
images of the repaired tear and the lining attachment. The images are stored on the
studio server under the folder `1987.114.2_2024-07-02_final`. A contact sheet has been
printed and placed in the treatment file.

2.2 Museum Director

The Museum Director is the chief executive officer, responsible for the day-to-day administration of the Museum, implementation of Board policy, and supervision of staff and operations. The Director reports directly to the Board of Trustees.

2.3 Staff and Volunteers

All staff and volunteers are expected to act in accordance with this Charter, the Museum's Code of Ethics, and applicable professional standards. Staff duties shall be defined by position descriptions, and volunteers shall operate under the supervision of appropriate staff members.

3. CODE OF ETHICS

3.1 General Principles

Oakridge Museum adheres to the principles set forth in the museum profession's Code of Ethics, which places the public trust at the center of all institutional activities. The Museum shall act with honesty, transparency, and integrity in all matters.

3.2 Collection Stewardship

The Museum's collections are held in the public trust. Staff shall:

- Acquire objects only through legal and ethical means, with clear title.
- Maintain accurate and complete records for all objects in the collection.
- Provide appropriate physical care and environmental conditions for collections.
- Make collections available for research, exhibition, and education while ensuring their long-term preservation.
- Exercise due diligence in considering the provenance of potential acquisitions.

3.3 Conflicts of Interest

Staff, trustees, and volunteers shall avoid conflicts of interest or the appearance thereof. Any actual or potential conflict shall be disclosed in writing to the Museum Director (for staff) or the Board Chair (for trustees). No individual shall use their position at the Museum for personal financial gain.

3.4 Intellectual Property and Copyright

The Museum shall respect the intellectual property rights of others and shall manage its own intellectual property responsibly. Reproduction of collection images and content shall follow established licensing procedures.

4. STRATEGIC GOALS (2024–2027)

The following strategic goals guide institutional planning for the current planning cycle:

4.1 Goal 1: Expand Community Engagement

Develop and sustain meaningful partnerships with local schools, cultural organizations, and community groups. Increase visitation among underserved populations by 15% over the planning period.

4.2 Goal 2: Enhance Collection Accessibility

Prioritize digitization of collections and expand online access. Complete the digitization of the photography and manuscript collections by the end of 2025.

4.3 Goal 3: Strengthen Financial Sustainability

Diversify revenue streams through increased membership, expanded grant funding, and the establishment of a planned giving program. Achieve a balanced operating budget by the end of the fiscal year.

4.4 Goal 4: Improve Operational Efficiency

Review and update internal procedures to streamline workflows and reduce administrative burden. Implement a new collections management system by early 2025.

**5. COLLECTION STEWARDSHIP PRINCIPLES (continued)**

**5.1 Provenance and Due Diligence**

The Museum shall maintain accurate, verifiable records of provenance for all objects in its
collection. Prior to any acquisition, whether by purchase, gift, bequest, or exchange, the
Curatorial Department shall conduct a due diligence review. This review shall include, where
practicable, consultation of available registries of stolen or illegally exported cultural
property, and shall be documented in the accession file. The Museum will not knowingly acquire
objects that have been illegally exported from their country of origin or that have been
unlawfully excavated.

**5.2 Deaccessioning**

Deaccessioning shall be undertaken only in accordance with the Museum’s stated purpose and
shall be a matter of public record. Funds derived from the sale of deaccessioned objects shall
be used solely for the acquisition of new objects or for the direct care of the collection,
as permitted by applicable law and professional standards. Any proposed deaccession shall be
reviewed by the Collections Committee and approved by the Board of Trustees. A record of all
deaccessions, including the rationale and the disposition of funds, shall be maintained
permanently.

**5.3 Loans**

Incoming and outgoing loans shall be governed by written loan agreements specifying duration,
condition reporting, insurance responsibilities, and permitted uses. The Registrar shall
coordinate all loan arrangements and shall maintain a loan register. Loans for exhibition,
study, or conservation shall be approved by the Curatorial Department. The Museum shall
ensure that all loaned objects are handled and stored to the same standards as its own
collections.

**5.4 Integrated Pest Management and Housekeeping**

The Facilities Department, in coordination with the Curatorial Department, shall implement an
integrated pest management program. This program shall include routine monitoring, sanitation
protocols, and documentation of any pest activity. A clean and stable environment is
essential for collection preservation; housekeeping schedules shall be maintained and
reviewed annually.

**6. PUBLIC ENGAGEMENT AND EDUCATION**

**6.1 Educational Programming**

The Museum is committed to providing educational opportunities for visitors of all ages and
backgrounds. The Education Department shall develop and deliver programs that interpret the
collections and support the Museum’s mission. Programs shall include guided tours, school
group visits, public lectures, workshops, and digital learning resources. The Education
Department shall collaborate with the Curatorial Department to ensure the accuracy of
interpretive content.

**6.2 Community Partnerships**

The Museum shall actively seek partnerships with local schools, historical societies,
cultural organizations, and community groups. These partnerships are intended to broaden
access to the collections and to ensure that the Museum’s programming reflects the diverse
interests of the community it serves. The Director of Education shall be responsible for
maintaining a current list of active partnerships and for reporting on their outcomes
annually.

**6.3 Visitor Experience**

The Museum shall strive to provide a welcoming and accessible environment for all visitors.
This includes maintaining clear signage, providing accessible routes and facilities, and
offering a variety of interpretive materials. Visitor feedback shall be collected
systematically and reviewed by the Visitor Services Manager, with a summary of findings
reported to the Museum Director quarterly.

Oakridge Museum
Visitor Guide: Hours, Admission, and Directions
Seasonal Update — Effective June 1, 2024

Welcome to Oakridge Museum! This guide covers everything you need to know for your visit, including hours, admission, getting here, parking, accessibility, and group visits. We update this brochure seasonally, so please check the date above to confirm you have the current version.

---

HOURS

Oakridge Museum has_operating_hours weekdays, 10:00-17:00, weekends, 12:00-18:00, closed, Mondays. Record status: current.

- Weekdays (Tue–Fri): 10:00 AM – 5:00 PM
- Weekends (Sat–Sun): 12:00 PM – 6:00 PM
- Mondays: Closed

Please note that the museum is closed on all major federal holidays, including Independence Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, and Christmas Day. On the day before a major holiday, the museum closes at 3:00 PM. Extended evening hours are offered on the first Thursday of each month (open until 8:00 PM) during June, July, and August. No extended hours are offered in other months.

Last admission is 45 minutes before closing time. Galleries begin closing in rotation 15 minutes prior to closing.

---

ADMISSION FEES

General Admission:
- Adults (18–64): $14
- Seniors (65+): $11
- Students (with valid ID): $11
- Youth (6–17): $7
- Children (5 and under): Free

Special Exhibitions:
- Included with general admission
- No additional ticket required

Members:
- Free general admission year-round
- Free admission to all special exhibitions

Free Admission Days:
- Third Saturday of each month: Free for all visitors
- Every Tuesday after 3:00 PM: Free for Oakridge County residents (proof of residency required)

Tickets may be purchased at the front desk, at the self-service kiosks in the main lobby, or online at oakridgemuseum.org/tickets. Online tickets are valid for any open day within 90 days of purchase. All sales are final; no refunds or exchanges.

---

DIRECTIONS

By Car:
- From Interstate 95, take Exit 42 (Oakridge Parkway) and head east for 2.5 miles. The museum is on the left, just past the Oakridge Public Library. Free parking is available in the museum lot.
- From downtown Oakridge, follow Main Street north for 1 mile, then turn right onto Museum Drive. The entrance is at the end of the drive.

By Bus:
- Oakridge Transit routes 7 and 12 stop at the museum entrance. Route 7 runs every 20 minutes on weekdays and every 30 minutes on weekends. Route 12 runs every 15 minutes on weekdays and every 25 minutes on weekends.
- The last bus departure from the museum stop is at 5:45 PM on weekdays and 6:45 PM on weekends. Plan your visit accordingly if you rely on public transit.

By Train:
- The Oakridge Station (Amtrak and commuter rail) is 1 mile south of the museum. A taxi stand is available outside the station, and ride-share pickups are located on the east side of the station. The walk from the station to the museum takes approximately 20 minutes along a paved, well-lit sidewalk.

By Bicycle:
- Bike racks are available on the east side of the main building, near the garden entrance. The Oakridge Greenway Trail connects directly to the museum grounds.

---

PARKING

Free parking is available for all visitors in the museum lot, which has 220 spaces. The lot is located directly in front of the main entrance. Accessible parking spaces are available near the entrance on a first-come, first-served basis.

Overflow parking is available at the Oakridge Public Library lot (2 blocks south) on weekends and during special events. Please observe all posted signs.

documents.title: Conservation Treatment Report: The Weaver Tapestry
documents.content:
The Weaver Tapestry is a hand-woven wool and silk tapestry, approximately 2.4 m (H) × 3.1 m (W), depicting a pastoral hunting scene. Warp: undyed linen, Z-twist, 8 threads/cm. Weft: wool, S-twist, with silk highlights in the foreground figures. The tapestry is comprised of three woven panels, joined edge-to-edge with a whip stitch. A linen lining (current) is attached along the top and sides; the bottom edge is unlined. A Velcro® attachment system is present along the top edge, with a secondary support of cotton webbing at the lower corners.

**2. CONDITION ASSESSMENT (performed 2025-01-15)**

**Overall:** Fair to poor. The tapestry is structurally sound but exhibits significant localized damage and active deterioration in the lower right quadrant.

**2.1. Structural Issues**

- **Warp Loss:** Two horizontal bands of warp loss are present in the lower right quadrant, measuring approximately 12 cm × 3 cm and 8 cm × 2.5 cm. The warp threads are broken and friable. Weft threads in these areas are exposed and lifting.
- **Slit Tapestry Seams:** The vertical slit seam between panel 2 and panel 3 has opened for a length of 45 cm, starting 60 cm from the bottom edge. The original silk binding threads are broken and partially detached.
- **Sagging / Distortion:** The lower left corner is sagging approximately 4 cm below the plane of the rest of the tapestry. This is likely due to the failure of a secondary support strap at that corner.

**2.2. Surface and Chemical Issues**

The Weaver Tapestry conservation status is undergoing treatment. Record status: current.

- **Fading:** The silk highlights in the foreground figures have faded significantly, with a noticeable color shift from a deep blue-green to a pale greenish-yellow. This is consistent with light damage. The wool background is relatively stable, though there is a lighter band (approx. 10 cm wide) along the top edge, likely from prior exposure to a skylight.
- **Stains:** A large, dark, irregular stain (approx. 20 cm × 15 cm) is present in the upper left quadrant, near the top edge. The stain is water-based and has a tide line. The origin is unknown; possibly a past roof leak. The dye in this area is partially solubilized.
- **Surface Dirt:** A uniform layer of surface dirt and soiling is present across the entire face, heavier in the lower half. There is a distinct, greasy deposit along the bottom edge, likely from handling and contact with a floor surface.
- **Previous Repairs:** A large, poorly executed repair is visible in the center of the tapestry, where a section of weft has been replaced with a modern synthetic thread (appears to be nylon) that has not been dyed to match. This repair is structurally sound but aesthetically disruptive. The thread is brittle and has a high gloss.

**2.3. Pest / Biological (no active infestation observed)**

- Old insect damage (likely carpet beetle) is present on the reverse, primarily along the bottom edge and in the area of the warp loss. The damage is historical and appears inactive. No frass or live insects were observed. A pest trap was placed near the object in storage; the last check (2024-11-20) was negative.

**2.4. Previous Treatment History**

- No prior conservation treatment documented in the current file. The object was examined on 2023-05-10 by a visiting consultant, but no treatment was performed. A note in the file indicates the tapestry was cleaned with a vacuum in 2019, but the method is not detailed.

**4. Progress Updates**

**4.1. Update 1 (2025-01-28)**

Initial surface cleaning has begun. The vacuum cleaning was completed on the face of the tapestry. The soiling was heavier than anticipated, especially in the lower half. The greasy deposit along the bottom edge responded well to the smoke sponge. The deposit appears to be a combination of dirt and a waxy substance, possibly from a floor polish. A small sample of the greasy deposit was taken for analysis (Sample ID: WT-2025-01). The analysis will be performed by the lab at the end of the week.

**4.2. Update 2 (2025-02-07)**

The stain reduction tests were conducted on the water stain. A small area (approx. 2 cm × 2 cm) was treated with deionized water using the suction disk. The test resulted in a slight reduction of the tide line, but the dye in the area is still partially solubilized. It was decided to proceed with a more localized treatment, using a cotton swab to apply the water directly to the stain, followed by immediate suction. This was performed on an area of the stain and has shown promising results. The full treatment of the stain is scheduled for next week. The analysis of the greasy deposit came back from the lab. It is a combination of a mineral oil and a synthetic wax, consistent with a floor polish. This information is useful; it suggests the tapestry was likely in contact with a floor that had been recently polished.

**4.3. Update 3 (2025-02-14)**

The reweaving of the area of the previous repair has been completed. The nylon thread was removed successfully. The surrounding warp threads were in good condition, which made the reweaving process straightforward. The new silk weft was dyed to match the surrounding wool. The color match is good, though it is slightly more saturated than the original. A note has been made in the file that the new repair will be re-evaluated after the tapestry has been on display for a period of time, as the dye may lighten. The Weaver Tapestry conservation treatment code is CT-2024-077. Record status: current. This code is current and should be used in all future correspondence regarding this object.

**5. Recommendations & Next Steps**

The next major step is the completion of the stain reduction treatment. Following that, the tapestry will be ready for the final inspection and photography. The estimated completion date for the treatment is 2025-03-14.

Once treatment is complete, the tapestry will be recommended for display. The lighting levels in the display area should be kept low (less than 50 lux) to prevent further fading of the silk highlights. The tapestry should be displayed on a padded support to prevent the formation of new creases. It is also recommended that the tapestry be placed in a climate-controlled environment with a relative humidity of 50% ± 5% and a temperature of 20°C ± 2°C.

A future treatment recommendation is to consider a more comprehensive cleaning of the reverse. The reverse was not cleaned as part of this treatment, as it was not a primary concern.

documents.title: Conservation Treatment Report: The Weaver Tapestry
documents.content:
**Conservation Treatment Report: The Weaver Tapestry**
**Accession No.:** 1987.114.2
**Object:** The Weaver Tapestry (wool, plain weave with supplemental weft)
**Treatment File No.:** TR-2024-061
**Conservator:** M. Rivera
**Dates of Treatment:** 2024-06-01 through 2024-06-28 (continuing)

---

**11. Progress Notes — Week of 2024-06-24**

**11.1. General**

Work continued on the lower right quadrant tear repair. The tear, measured at 12 inches
along the warp direction, has been stabilized. The loose warp ends were aligned and
secured with a temporary stitch using undyed silk thread (50/3) prior to the application
of the patch. The patch was cut from the dyed cotton lining fabric prepared earlier in
the treatment; the fabric was dyed to match the reverse of the tapestry. The patch was
pinned in place and will be stitched in the next session.

The decision to add a removable lining, noted in the examination notes (Section 10.2),
was reviewed. The cotton fabric selected for the lining was washed and dyed on
2024-06-19. After dyeing, the fabric was rinsed until the water ran clear and then
air-dried. A small sample of the dyed fabric was retained for the treatment record and
is stored in a Mylar sleeve in the treatment file.

**11.2. Fringe Assessment**

The fringe along the bottom edge was re-examined. The earlier note (2024-06-01)
indicating that the fringe was "missing in sections" was corrected in the database;
the fringe is present but was folded under the hem. The fringe is in fair condition,
with some breakage and loss of twist. The fringe will be gently cleaned with a soft
brush and a HEPA-filtered vacuum at low suction. No further treatment is planned for
the fringe at this time.

**11.3. Photography**

Digital photographs were taken on 2024-06-25 to document the progress of the tear
repair. Images were captured before and after the application of the temporary
stitches. Photographs were taken under raking light to highlight the weave structure
and the area of the repair. Images are stored on the studio server under the folder
`1987.114.2_2024-06-25`. A contact sheet was printed and placed in the treatment
file.

**11.4. Dye Analysis — Additional Samples**

In addition to the initial HPLC analysis (Section 10.2), a sample of the blue yarn
from the central medallion was analyzed on 2024-06-24. The analysis confirmed the
presence of indigo. A sample of the red yarn from the border was also analyzed; the
results indicated the presence of madder. No synthetic dyes were detected in either
sample. The results are consistent with the initial analysis.

**12. Treatment Proposal — Lining and Support**

The following treatment steps are proposed for the next phase of treatment. This
proposal supersedes the preliminary plan outlined in the initial examination notes,
specifically regarding the method of attachment for the lining.

**12.1. Lining Attachment**

The lining will be attached using a series of vertical stitches along the sides and
bottom of the tapestry. The stitches will be made with the undyed silk thread (50/3)
and will be spaced approximately 2 inches apart. The top edge will be left open to
allow for future inspection. This method is a change from the initial plan, which
called for a full perimeter stitch. The revised method will reduce stress on the
selvages.

**12.2. Patch Stitching**

The patch for the tear will be stitched with a curved needle using a running stitch.
The stitch will be placed approximately 1/4 inch from the edge of the tear. The
stitches will be made with the undyed silk thread.

documents.content:
**13. Treatment Progress — Lining and Support (continued)**

**13.1. Lining Fabric Preparation**

The linen lining fabric (accession file note: 1987.114.2 lining, bolt L-4) was washed and
ironed on 2024-06-27. The fabric was cut to size, allowing a 3-inch turnover on all four
sides. The cut edges were finished with a rolled hem to prevent fraying during handling.
The prepared lining is currently stored rolled, not folded, on a padded tube in the
studio’s textile storage area. The rolled storage is to prevent creasing that could
interfere with the final drape of the tapestry.

**13.2. Stitch Spacing Verification**
